title: Is a Documentary True?
objective: After this level you can weigh how choices of framing, editing and reenactment can shape a documentary's truth without inventing facts.
summary: Documentary is the creative treatment of actuality. Framing, sets, music and reenactment shape it; The Thin Blue Line staged accounts honestly and helped free a man.

cards.headline: A documentary full of staged scenes helped free a man from death row.
cards.body: Errol Morris's The Thin Blue Line (1988) argued that Randall Dale Adams, on death row for killing a Texas police officer, was innocent. It played a major role in his release. It also staged the crime again and again. How can staging serve the truth?

cards.headline: Creative treatment of actuality
cards.body: Documentary pioneer John Grierson described documentary as creative treatment of actuality. Real events, but a filmmaker chooses the frame, the order and the sound. Some shaping goes further: Night Mail (1936) intercut real footage of the mail train with scenes shot on elaborate studio sets, much as Level 19's Nanook used a second igloo with a wall removed for the camera.

cards.headline: Staging the accounts, not the answer
cards.body: The Thin Blue Line reviewed Adams's case. Morris's staged scenes don't show what he believed happened; they show each witness's conflicting account so you can grasp each one. Philip Glass's score often plays under the interviews, adding an emotional inflection. The film played a major role in Adams's release in 1989.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 94's test works here too. Imagine the same testimony without Glass's score.

cards.headline: Shaping or inventing?
cards.body: So how do you judge? Ask two questions of any scene: what does it claim to show, and is that claim true? A staged scene presented as one witness's account can be honest. A staged moment passed off as plain fact is not: Level 19's Nanook showed two women as Nanook's wives who weren't his wives. Shaping is every documentary's job. Inventing facts is where the truth breaks.

cards.headline: Is a Documentary True?: done
learned: Sets and reenactments shape real events
Staging accounts differs from inventing facts
The Thin Blue Line helped free Adams

questions.prompt: Put these documentary moments in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Night Mail came out in 1936, The Thin Blue Line in 1988, and Randall Dale Adams was released in 1989.

questions.prompt: Why can The Thin Blue Line's reenactments be defended as honest?

options.label: They show the one true version of the crime that Morris later proved in court
options.rationale: Morris staged each witness's account, not his own verdict.

options.label: They show each witness's conflicting account, not a claimed true version
They were filmed on the night of the crime
They have no music, so they can't steer you
options.rationale: Glass's score does add emotion to the testimony.

questions.explanation: The staged scenes depict each witness's version so viewers can grasp and compare them.

questions.prompt: Nanook of the North's 'wives' weren't his wives. How does that differ from The Thin Blue Line's staged scenes?

options.label: It doesn't: both films honestly show every witness's own account of real events
options.rationale: Nanook presented an arranged family as his own.

options.label: Nanook used no staging at all
options.rationale: The igloo, the family and the seal hunt were arranged.

options.label: Nanook invented a fact about his life, while Morris staged accounts as accounts
Morris used actors, so his film is fiction
options.rationale: Staging accounts clearly doesn't make a documentary fiction.

questions.explanation: Presenting two women as a man's wives when they weren't invents a fact; staging each witness's version shapes without inventing.
